decks.name: AI Words Explained Simply
decks.description: AI words explained the way you'd tell a 5-year-old — short, clear, no jargon.

cards.definition: A way to talk to a computer by typing instead of clicking. You type what you want, press Enter, and the computer does it.
A rule book that lets a smart helper plug into your apps. Like how a USB cable lets any keyboard work with any computer.
A really good guessing machine that read most of the internet. You give it some words, and it guesses the next ones — really, really well.
A tiny piece of a word. The computer doesn't see whole words — it sees little chunks, like cutting a sandwich into bites.
How much the computer can think about at once. Like how many toys you can hold — once your hands are full, you have to drop something.
Turning words into numbers so the computer knows which words mean similar things. Like sorting LEGO bricks by color.
A special box that finds the bits of text that look most like the one you have. Like finding all the puzzle pieces that match a certain color.
Before the computer answers, it looks stuff up. Like checking a book before answering a question.
A robot helper that doesn't just talk. It actually does things — opens files, sends messages, runs programs.
Letting the computer grab other helpers when it needs them. Like using a calculator instead of doing the math by hand.
Teaching a smart computer a few extra tricks so it gets really good at one specific job.
What you type to tell the computer what you want.
A secret note the computer reads first. It tells the helper who to be and what rules to follow.
Showing the computer a few examples first so it copies the pattern. Like saying 'here are three cats — draw me a fourth.'
Telling the computer 'think out loud, step by step' so it gets the right answer instead of guessing.
When the computer makes stuff up that sounds real but isn't true.
A dial for how wild the computer's answers are. Low = boring and exact. High = fun and surprising.
A way to stop the computer from picking really weird words. It only chooses from the words most likely to come next.
Like top-p but simpler. Pick from the top few words, no matter what.
Training where people say 'I like this answer better' over and over, until the computer learns what humans prefer.
Squishing a huge smart model into a smaller one so it fits on a phone or laptop. It loses a tiny bit of smarts but runs much faster.
When the computer actually answers your question. (Not when it's learning — that's training.)
How long you wait for an answer. Lower is better.
How many answers the computer can give at the same time.
Safety fences. They keep the computer from saying or doing things it shouldn't.
A helper that can see pictures, hear sounds, AND read words — not just one of those.
A special kind of computer brain that's really good at language. Almost every AI chatbot uses one.
A huge, general-purpose AI brain. Other people build smaller, more specific helpers on top of it.
The newest date the computer knows about. Stuff that happened after that date? It has no idea.
A computer that thinks longer and harder before answering. Like a kid carefully working through a math problem on paper.
Instead of one giant brain answering everything, lots of smaller expert brains take turns — whichever one knows best for the question.
The trick that lets the computer focus on the important words and ignore the rest. Like underlining the key sentence in a paragraph.
A small add-on that teaches a big model a new trick — without changing the big model itself.
Teaching a smaller, faster model everything a big slow model knows. Like a student copying the teacher.
How most AI image-makers work: start with random noise, then slowly clean it up until a picture appears.
Trying to trick the helper by sneaking secret instructions into something it reads.
Tricking the helper into doing something it was told not to.
Showing the answer word-by-word as it's being typed, instead of waiting for the whole thing.
A door other programs use to talk to the AI. You knock with a question, the AI sends an answer back.
When the company who built the model shares the brain itself, so anyone can run it on their own computer.
A test to see how good the computer is at a job. Like a school exam, but for AI.
A super-fast chip that's great at the math AI needs. Originally built for video games.
